questions.q: In Chromium, what does an element with id="settings" become on window?
o: A string copy of that element's inner text content
A property window.settings that points at that node
A CSS custom property named --settings on :root
A cookie whose name is settings for the same origin
questions.x: Chromium exposes a top-level element with id="settings" as window.settings. The value is the DOM node, not a config object. A page that reads window.settings || defaults can then skip the fallback, because a node is truthy.
questions.h: Named access on window turns some HTML ids into global properties. What type of value is window.settings in that case?

questions.q: In Chromium, what is window.foo when two elements share id="foo"?
o: Always only the first matching node in the tree
Often an HTMLCollection that lists both of those nodes
A Map object whose keys are the two element tags
undefined, because duplicate ids get ignored entirely
questions.x: Duplicate ids often make window.foo an HTMLCollection of both nodes. Named items in that collection can be read like object properties. That is how HTML can fake a nested shape without any script tag.
questions.h: One id maps to one node. What does Chromium often expose when the same id appears twice?

questions.q: How can two anchors fake an object shape like { theme: "dark" }?
o: Nest one anchor inside the other so href becomes a child key
Give both the same id, and put name="theme" href="dark" on one
Set data-theme="dark" on a single div that has id="opts"
Use a form with method="GET" plus an input named theme
questions.x: Two anchors with id="opts", one also having name="theme" href="dark", can make window.opts an HTMLCollection. In Chromium, window.opts.theme is often the string "dark" from href. Nested parent and child anchors are not what creates that collection.
questions.h: Chromium's fake object shape uses duplicate ids plus a name and href on an anchor, not nesting.

questions.q: How does Firefox differ from Chromium on duplicate-id clobbering?
o: Firefox never maps any element id onto a window property
Firefox keeps a single node, not an HTMLCollection of both
Firefox maps ids onto window but only inside nested iframes
Firefox treats duplicate ids as a syntax error and then stops
questions.x: Firefox still clobbers flat names, so one element with id="foo" can be window.foo and skip a || fallback. Duplicate ids stay the first matching node, not an HTMLCollection, so window.foo.bar from a second element's name and href does not resolve the Chromium way.
questions.h: Firefox still maps a single id onto window. What does it refuse to do with two nodes that share that id?

questions.q: Why can const settings = window.settings || defaults skip the fallback?
o: window.settings is always a string, and strings are falsy
A clobbered DOM node is truthy, so the || right side never runs
let and const bindings always overwrite window.settings first
The || operator only runs when the left side is an object
questions.x: || only treats missing or empty values as a miss. A DOM node is truthy, so the hardcoded defaults never apply. A top-level let or const named settings would not collide with window.settings, but this lookup is a property read on window.
questions.h: The check is 'is window.settings missing or empty?' Is a DOM element missing, or is it a real truthy value?
